title: Learning Go, and someone else's codebase, under pressure
question: Tell me about a time you were pushed outside your comfort zone

situation: AWS Lambda had an existing Java path that optimised ZIP function packages, with and without layers, and transformed them into the format expected by the data plane. Parts of that flow were still synchronous and largely stateless, while the asynchronous path relied on S3 notifications that could trigger duplicate Lambda invocations and required workarounds to ignore redundant work.
I joined after the initiative had already started. The codebase was unfamiliar to me, and Go, the language chosen for the replacement, was new to me as well.
task: I was asked to design and implement a high-performance replacement in Go that could support both SQS-driven and direct HTTP execution, and later to help refactor the control plane orchestration around function layers and artifact storage.
The challenge was to learn a new language and an unfamiliar production system quickly, while redesigning a critical processing path without disrupting the existing flow during migration.
action: I first traced the existing Java workflow end to end to understand the business behaviour we needed to preserve and the implementation constraints we could remove. I used integration tests as a safety net while learning both the codebase and Go.

I designed the replacement as a concurrent, channel-based pipeline, allowing independent processing stages to run in parallel. I also designed the interfaces so the same processing pipeline could be driven through either SQS or direct HTTP.

The execution model was particularly important because our Lambda workers were intentionally short-lived for customer isolation and governance reasons: different customers could not share process memory, so each invocation had to be treated as an isolated unit of work. The lightweight Go implementation helped keep that model efficient, while the new parallelism reduced the time spent waiting on independent processing stages.

As I became more familiar with the system, I was asked to join an away team working on the surrounding control plane orchestration. I ended up rewriting most of that component, adding proper support for function layers and several edge cases around artifact fetching and storage.
I also built a rapid integration-testing framework so we could exercise complete workflows and safely validate the migration.
result: The new pipeline roughly halved end-to-end package processing latency, primarily through the new parallel execution model combined with the efficiency of the Go-based, short-lived Lambda workers.
The work also expanded into ownership of a significant part of the surrounding control plane, with automated integration coverage protecting the function layers and orchestration edge cases.

challenge: The hardest part was learning the system while changing it. I had to understand a large unfamiliar codebase, ramp up on Go and its concurrency model, and still make changes to a production-critical flow where mistakes could affect Lambda function creation and updates.
hardestBug: During rollout, the team reused an existing image-function polling mechanism to copy artifacts for newly created function versions. That approach had worked at the old scale, but ZIP functions increased the volume dramatically. In our largest region, redundant copies started overwhelming the background processing path and affected image functions as well, threatening control plane operations and blocking global rollout.
I designed a deduplication mechanism and the corresponding background-job changes within about a week, removing the redundant copies and allowing the rollout to continue safely.
differently: I would introduce realistic load and noisy-neighbour testing earlier. Our functional integration coverage was strong, but it did not reproduce the scale and concurrency of the largest regions. A synthetic stress environment would likely have exposed the background-job scaling limits before production rollout.
aboutYourself: I learned that I do not need to understand an entire unfamiliar system before I can contribute meaningfully to it. Breaking the problem into data flows, validating assumptions with tests, and asking targeted questions made a codebase that initially felt overwhelming progressively manageable.
enjoyed: I enjoyed the combination of learning and design: getting comfortable with Go's concurrency model, reasoning about the end-to-end distributed workflow, and working directly with principal engineers in the US on the harder architectural trade-offs.
